title: Age-Appropriate Chores: Full 2-to-18 List by Age
meta_description: What chores are age-appropriate at every stage, 2 to 18, from a dad of four and foster parent. Pick your child's age for a free chart built for them.
intro: If you've ever wondered what your kid should actually be doing around the house at their age, you're asking the right question — and you're in the right place. Age-appropriate chores aren't a single list you hand down; they're a sequence that grows up alongside your child, looking almost nothing alike at 3 versus 13. I'm Andrew, and between our own four kids (right now spanning 9 to 18) and three little ones we fostered as toddlers, we've watched that whole arc play out more than once. Below, you can pick any age to jump straight to a chart built for that stage. But first, here's the part most lists leave out: why the jobs change the way they do, and how to choose a starting point your child can actually live up to. A quick promise — none of this rests on stickers or paying per task. In our home the reason a kid pitches in is simply that they're part of the family, and families pull together.

sections.heading: What to expect at each stage, from toddler to teen
sections.body:
Think of age-appropriate chores in roughly four chapters, each with a different point.

The earliest years, around 2 to 4, aren't really about housework. They're about a child learning to manage their own body and belongings — dressing themselves, handling teeth, gathering up the toys they dumped out. The trick at this age is invitation, not assignment: if your toddler reaches for the broom because you're sweeping, hand it over and show them a single move. You won't get a clean floor. You'll get a kid who, two years from now, doesn't flinch when you ask for help.

The early-school years, say 5 through 7, are when a job becomes a job. We start folding in shared-space tasks here — a bathroom counter, the table, feeding a pet. Set your expectations low at first. The work will be wobbly and you'll often go behind them to finish it. That's fine, because the real lesson at this age isn't a spotless sink; it's that the house belongs to everyone in it, and everyone has a hand in keeping it running.

The middle years, roughly 8 to 12, are where ability finally meets expectation. Now we're talking real dishes, taking out trash, helping cook a meal, and for the ones who gravitate toward it, yard work and hands-on projects. Our son will trail me through any repair, peppering me with questions, and you can watch competence build in real time. The chores get harder because the kid can handle harder.

The teen years are a different game entirely, and I'll be straight with you: the wall chart that worked at 8 falls apart around 13. We've now guided two kids through their teens with two more on the way. The shift is from a tracked chore list to something that functions more like adult responsibility — agreed-on contributions, more autonomy, and far less hovering. The teen page digs into exactly how we restructured it once the chart stopped doing its job.

sections.heading: How to choose your child's starting point
sections.body:
Age is your first clue, not your final answer. Picking the age above gives you a chart that fits the typical abilities of that stage, and for most families that's the right place to begin.

But read the kid in front of you. If chores are brand new to your household, or if you've watched a past chart die on the fridge, set the bar one notch below their age rather than at it. A nine-year-old who has never been held to a routine will do far better growing into the eight-year-old list than drowning in one written for his age. Moving the bar up later is easy and feels like a win; pulling a frustrated kid back down from a list that's beating them is a much harder conversation.

This is something fostering taught us in a way our own kids never could. The three toddlers we cared for arrived without the steady rhythms a lot of children take for granted, and for them, a routine they could count on did more heavy lifting than any single task ever did. When the same small steps happened in the same order day after day, they relaxed into it — and you could see the trust and the self-control start to take root. It convinced me that the goal isn't an impressive list. It's a level your child can meet again and again, because that dependable repetition is what turns chores into something that actually sticks. So pick an age, give it a week or two, and nudge it upward once it starts to feel easy.

sections.heading: The philosophy: a tracking tool for you, not a bribe for them
sections.body:
Every per-age chart on this site shares one belief, so I want to name it directly. The chart is there to help you, the parent, keep an honest read on how each child is doing and to flag when it's time to step in. It is not a machine for buying cooperation.

That distinction changes your move when motivation sags. The instinct is to sweeten the deal — a bigger prize, a screen-time carrot. We go the other way and lean back on the expectation itself: in this house everyone pitches in, and that isn't up for negotiation. We keep treats, fun, and screens deliberately walled off from the chore list. We don't ask our kids to earn their downtime by working, and we don't price chores out one by one like items at a checkout.

Allowance does exist in our home, but it isn't a per-job payout. It's tied to the bigger picture — whether the work is done with care, done reliably, and done with a decent attitude over time. The moment chores become a transaction, kids learn to ask what's in it for them. When chores are simply part of belonging to a family, that question quietly disappears, and the chart goes back to being what it should be: your tool for seeing the whole picture.

faq.q: What chores are age-appropriate for kids at each age?
faq.a: Broadly: ages 2 to 4 center on self-care like dressing, brushing teeth, and picking up their own mess. Ages 5 to 7 add light shared-space jobs such as wiping a counter or setting the table, with results you'll often redo. Ages 8 to 12 handle dishes, trash, cooking help, and outdoor work as their skill grows. Teens move to bigger, more independent responsibilities. Pick your child's exact age above to see the specific list built for that stage instead of guessing.

faq.q: At what age should a child start doing chores?
faq.a: You can begin around 2 to 3, but at that point it's really self-care plus letting them 'help' without requiring it — you're building familiarity, not getting useful work done. Chores you actually assign and track tend to take hold around 5 to 6, once a child can understand they're a contributing member of the household. In our home that's also when a small, attitude-based allowance enters the picture, kept separate from paying per task.

faq.q: Should I base chores on my child's age or their ability?
faq.a: Start with age to get a developmentally sensible baseline, then adjust for the real kid. If your child is new to chores or a previous chart fell apart, drop down one level so they can succeed consistently, then raise it as the work gets easy. We learned — especially through fostering — that dependable repetition matters more than an ambitious list. A level a child can hit every single day beats a stretch list that ends up ignored.
